stories.title: Talks to resolve Drumcree dispute end without agreement
stories.summary: Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement, as a legal appeal over the contentious march is scheduled for Monday. Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant described the situation as being between a "rock and a hard place" after unsuccessful late-night negotiations at Hillsborough Castle with representatives from the Orange Order and Garvaghy Road residents on what was the fifth day of the stand-off. The Portadown District of the unionist Orange Order wants to complete its traditional route for the first time in almost 30 years after the Parades Commission ruled they should be allowed along the Garvaghy Road, but the coalition of residents in the largely nationalist area is opposed to the march going ahead. Mr Bryant told reporters his door remained open for further discussion, but said: "This is the end of these conversations. "We haven't come to a settled agreement and it's a shame but my door remains open obviously, tomorrow and in future days. "We've discussed a wide range of options, including mediation, including an option where the right to march was respected but wasn't exercised, including an option where there was a final march and no further applications for marches into the future, and we've not managed to come to agreement on any of all that."

stories.title: Residents discuss proposal, DUP MP says deal unacceptable
stories.summary: A proposed deal to resolve the Drumcree parading dispute is "not acceptable", a DUP MP has said. Carla Lockhart's assessment came after a representative of the Garvaghy Road residents said they would accept a document setting out a resolution if the Orange Order also did so. Breandán Mac Cionnaith was speaking following a meeting with British Secretary of State for Northern Ireland Chris Bryant at Hillsborough Castle. Mr Bryant has been trying to strike a compromise deal between the two sides of the standoff. Mr Mac Cionnaith said: "Obviously I can’t divulge what is in it but if it’s accepted by the Orange Order, it will be accepted by us." Portadown Orange Order district master Nigel Dawson declined to comment on the paper as he left the castle this evening.

stories.title: SF alternative budget targets living costs, second homes
stories.summary: Sinn Féin is proposing a permanent ten cent reduction in petrol and diesel as well as extending excise cuts for another six months as part of its €13.4 billion alternative budget package. The 40-page document, entitled 'Putting workers and families first', proposes the Government not proceed with planned carbon tax increases, remove all excise on home heating oil and reduce green diesel by 17 cent for a minimum of six months. The proposed measures to help reduce fuel costs for households run to €1.5 billion with the expense of cutting 10c off petrol and diesel at the pumps for the next year running to €404 million. As per last year, Sinn Féin is proposing an emergency cost of living package. This would include an "Everyday Essential Card" - a preloaded card with €500 for one million households most in need to spend on groceries - and the extension of the back-to-school clothing and footwear allowance to every child in the country. The party would also provide €400 in energy credits for householders. Sinn Féin would also abolish student fees, halt public transport fare increases and introduce a new tier of child benefit to target those most at risk of poverty.

stories.title: Ryanair passenger numbers rise by 4% in September
stories.summary: Ryanair has today announced a 4% increase in passenger numbers for September as it operated over 111,700 flights during the month. Ryanair said it carried a total of 20.1 million passengers last month, up from 19.4 million during the same month last year. The airline's load factor - how many seats it fills on each flight - was steady at 94%. Ryanair said it was forced to cancel over 1,000 flights due to problems with the UK air traffic control system, Belgian air traffic control strikes and the Mout Etna eruptions.

stories.title: Bins set alight and trams halted as French pupils protest
stories.summary: A high-school entrance hall caught fire in one French city and teenage protesters blocked trams in another as secondary pupils upped their strike over what they denounce as poor learning conditions. The movement in the lycees, which students aged 15 to 18 attend for their final three years of secondary education in France, has seen hundreds detained in recent days. Since last week, pupils have staged protests outside schools over grievances ranging from timetables, class sizes and a shortage of teachers to overheated classrooms during this year's heatwaves. The protests have spread across the country from the Paris suburbs, with the government accusing hard-left politicians of encouraging the unrest. Riot police were deployed to confront the students, with the force launching internal probes after accusations of brutality against three pupils, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nunez. Around 340 demonstrations were under way in front of high schools by the mid-morning, with more than 160 establishments shut down as a result, police said.

stories.title: Munster looking forward as Flanagan falls on his sword
stories.summary: It seemed inevitable that there would be change at the top of Munster Rugby after the Roger Randle saga in April. The only surprise is that it took close to six months for it to happen, with CEO Ian Flanagan confirming on Thursday that he will resign at the end of October. When an independent report into the governance of Munster Rugby was commissioned in May, it appeared as if Flanagan had bought himself time to weather the storm after what had been a damaging couple of months for the province. The findings of that report are yet to be made public, although the review, which was conducted by The Governance Company, was expected to be delivered to the province by the end of September. Upon launching the review, which issued confidential surveys to a wide range of both internal and external stakeholders, independent chair Martin Kelleher said it would be "looking forward in nature", adding that it was "not an investigation, a disciplinary process or a fault-finding exercise, and it does not seek to attribute blame to individuals". While the review may have been "looking forward", it was hard not to join the dots between it and the farcical Roger Randle saga, which played out just a few weeks earlier.

stories.title: Fitzmaurice appointed Galway manager on three-year term
stories.summary: Former Kerry manager Éamonn Fitzmaurice has been appointed the manager of the Galway senior footballers on a three-year term, having been ratified at a meeting of the county board on Wednesday night. The Kerry man takes over the role, succeeding Pádraic Joyce who left the fold earlier this month. A three-time All-Ireland winner as a player, Fitzmaurice managed Kerry for six years between 2013 and 2018, leading the Kingdom to Sam Maguire glory in 2014. He also claimed six straight Munster SFC titles and an Allianz League title during his time in charge. He remained involved with the club scene in his native Kerry, coaching the Clifford brothers' club Fossa in 2022 as they claimed a junior All-Ireland title. Fitzmaurice also formed part of the Football Review Committee chaired by Jim Gavin, who was also believed to have interviewed for the job.

stories.title: Preview: Ireland to face pressing questions from Austria
stories.summary: For Heimir Hallgrimsson, one short aside on Wednesday highlighted what the Republic of Ireland manager would ideally have wanted to speak about on the eve of a match. "We are in a pre-match press conference before a game against Austria and we have hardly ever spoken about football here," he said. But this has been a window like no other. As expected, the tenor of the pre-match press conference questions was going to focus on the controversial UEFA Nations League fixtures against Israel and the fallout from Saturday's acrimonious build-up to the first of those matches in Debrecen. The Israel issue will still be front and centre again tonight at Aviva Stadium. The Stop The Game campaign have promised that protests will take place around the game with the visiting Austrians. Four months ago, the same campaign staged a tennis ball protest in the same venue during a friendly against Qatar. It's unclear what shape tonight's protests will take, nor what the overall attendance figures will be. And that's not even to countenance how players will be received individually and collectively from those in the stands.

stories.title: Second row O'Tighearnaigh on juggling medicine and rugby
stories.summary: Conor O'Tighearnaigh could be said to represent something of a throwback. Back in the days when playing rugby was officially a hobby for even those at the highest level, there were plenty of doctors and would-be doctors in the international game. Ireland's greatest player of the pre-professional era, Jack Kyle, worked as a surgeon in Africa for decades. In the professional era, the likes of Felipe Contepomi and Jamie Roberts have combined medical studies with a rugby career. But it's a rare enough combo these days, making Leinster second row O'Tighearnaigh's juggling of the two all the more notable, especially as he attempts to break into the starting team. The 23-year old former St Michael's student, who was part of the Ireland Under-20 Grand Slam winning teams in 2022 and 2023, featured in the pack in Leinster's narrow loss to the Lions in Johannesburg last week. The trip to South Africa has forced a slight pause in his medical training, where he is currently on placement at St Vincent's hospital in Dublin - but he'll catch up soon enough. "I'm now doing it on a stretched-out basis," O'Tighearnaigh said. "I did the first four years full whack. Last year, I took a leave of absence from medicine.

stories.title: Everyone is a writer now — but what does being a writer mean?
stories.summary: I've taught creative writing for years, in universities, writers’ centres, libraries and festivals, online and in person, and the people who come to these courses are always wildly different. Some have been writing for decades, others have barely written anything since school and arrive nervous, apologising before they have even read a sentence aloud. Some are hugely talented and some are not, which is a difficult and sometimes unpopular thing to say, but it makes it no less true. More and more, the conversation turns towards publication. How do I get an agent? How do I know when the novel is ready? Why am I still being rejected? People tell me they have done five courses, ten courses, an MA, sometimes another MA, and are confused that nothing has happened. They have spent the money, taken the feedback and rewritten the novel. Surely they should be published by now. I understand the ambition. I did an undergraduate degree in English, then a Masters in Creative Writing, then a PhD in Creative Writing, which is a ridiculous amount of time to spend studying something that guarantees no job or success at the end of it. I wrote a novel that went out to publishers and received beautiful rejections, editors writing long emails about what they admired before explaining that they would not be publishing it. Not everyone who writes will be published, and not everyone who writes should be. That does not mean they should stop. That novel remains unpublished. During the years I spent writing it, I was working, teaching, living abroad, getting married and having children. I was building a life that did not look as though it would include being a novelist. Still, I wasn’t waiting for my real life to begin. I loved books, was thirsty for knowledge and wanted to write better. The novel going nowhere doesn’t take that away.

stories.title: Joanne McNally competes in Celebrity Traitors UK
stories.summary: Joanne McNally is competing in the British version of Celebrity Traitors, which ended on a cliffhanger with James Acaster and Amol Rajan fighting for their lives after just the first episode. The BBC series hosted by by Claudia Winkleman, follows 21 celebrity contestants as they try to seek out the traitors among them who kill off players in the middle of the night. In the first episode, The Scarlet Pimpernel actor Richard E Grant, 69, and Love Island host Maya Jama, 32, were the first two chosen as traitors. However, by the end of the episode they were told they had a chance to recruit – and could kill another contestant at the same time. They selected British comedian Acaster, 41, and University Challenge presenter Rajan, 43, who had to meet the two traitors face to face and were challenged with pleading their case. Both said they could help deflect attention for Grant after he accidentally revealed to multiple people he was a traitor, with the episode ending before the traitors selected who to save.

stories.title: Ban on use of e-scooters for under 18s comes into force
stories.summary: A ban on the use of e-scooters for under-18s comes into effect today, just four weeks after new regulations requiring e-scooter users to wear helmets and high visibility clothing came into force. Compliance with those new measures appears to be very low but the Minister for Transport Darragh O'Brien has said that while it takes time for new rules to bed in, he is "watching carefully" how people are responding to the new regulations. Up to now, the minimum age for e-scooter use was 16, but as of today, that has been increased to 18, making the use of an e-scooter by a child illegal. Fees for the detention and storage of seized e-scooters also doubles from today to an initial €80, increasing by €30 a day thereafter. These new rules around scooters were introduced after medics in CHI Temple Street called for an outright ban on their use because of the high number of children they were seeing coming into their Emergency Department critically injured from e-scooter related injuries. In one fortnight period in early July, six children were put on life support in that one Dublin hospital due to injuries they sustained from e-scooters.

stories.title: 5% of Ireland job postings mention data centres - Indeed
stories.summary: Just under 5% of all job postings on the Indeed hiring platform now mention data centres. This is roughly double the percentage share seen between 2019 and 2025 and, according to Indeed, the highest proportion among ten European countries analysed by the platform. Indeed's research also found that European employers advertise higher pay for data centre roles than for the same occupations elsewhere. "The largest premiums are generally seen among workers directly tied to data centre sites, including installation and maintenance roles," according to Indeed. Pawel Adrjan, Senior Director of Economic Research for EMEA and APAC at Indeed, said data centre hiring is one of the few areas of growth in tech-adjacent hiring at a time when wider tech postings remain under pressure. "Ireland stands out particularly strongly, with nearly 5% of job postings now mentioning a data centre, roughly twice the share we have seen in recent years," Mr Adrjan said.

stories.title: SDLP selects new candidate for Justin McNulty seat
stories.summary: Councillor Peter Byrne will contest Newry and Armagh for the SDLP in next year's Assembly convention, replacing Justin McNulty. Mr Byrne, a councillor for 10 years, was chosen in a selection convention of party members. He runs a business in Crossmaglen, where he lives with his husband. Following his selection, he said he wants to be "a relentless champion for Newry and Armagh". In an apparent reference to the Drumcree dispute, he added: "If the past week teaches us anything, it is that we need to move forward and do politics differently. "For the SDLP, that means making things work today whilst planning for a new Ireland in the future, and I am looking forward to taking this message to the people of Newry and Armagh in the weeks and months ahead."

stories.title: JD Wetherspoon flags good start to year from hot weather
stories.summary: British pub chain J D Wetherspoon has today posted an 8.6% rise in like-for-like sales at the start of its fiscal 2027, as hot weather drew more customers to its facilities. The heatwave helped lift consumer spending, offering a respite for Britain's hospitality sector as it contends with elevated tax, labour and energy costs. Wetherspoon, which issued four profit warnings this year, reported a 28% fall in pretax profit before separately disclosed items to £58.6m for the year ended July 26.

stories.title: US government's new AI chatbot stops debunking Trump
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump unveiled what he called a "damn good" AI chatbot, but it quickly drew attention for contradicting some of his contentious political claims. A day later, however, it stopped answering some political questions. "Hello, America. Whatever you need from government, start here," reads the America.gov platform, which Mr Trump launched in a bid to simplify access to government information and federal services. The chatbot soon began contradicting Mr Trump on controversial subjects such as the 2020 presidential election, which he wrongly claims to have won, and the 6 January 2021 insurrection that saw a violent mob attacking the US Capitol. "On its first day, America.gov harnessed facts and official documents to contradict some of the false narratives and political framing about immigration and elections heavily promoted by the administration that built it," said the Digital Democracy Institute of the Americas. "Initial analyses found that America.gov generally provided evidence-based answers backed by government records, even when those records contradicted claims made by Trump and his administration."

stories.title: Hallgrimsson sees positives as 'tiredness' halts Ireland
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson has pointed to fatigue as the reason his squad squandered a two-goal lead to draw 2-2 with Austria on Thursday. A Troy Parrott wonder goal gave Ireland the lead early into the game, before the Real Betis striker added a second from the penalty spot before the break. However, goals from Alexander Prass and Michael Gregoritsch within six minutes of one another ended Irish hopes of topping the group at the halfway stage of the UEFA Nations League B group phase. "We knew, and I told you before the game, this team is high energy; and we knew that we needed to do some rotation and changes. I felt like we just lost organisation, probably due to tiredness, and then you start to make mistakes. "That was something that we were obviously not happy with, but the first half was good, the organisation was good, we know we can do this. "I kind of expected us to get out of gas at some point, but maybe not so quickly. This week has been not only physically difficult, (but) it's been mentally difficult and that takes a lot of energy as well."

stories.title: McStay hopeful of 'five or six' new rules for 2027 league
stories.summary: Gaelic football's Expert Advisory Group (EAG) chairman Kevin McStay is hopeful that "five or six" new rules will be officially adopted in time for the 2027 Allianz Football League - but he said that the changes will have to meet "a high threshold" to form part of the official guidelines. EAG members McStay, Séamus Kenny and Johnny Bradley addressed the media at Croke Park on Wednesday and provided more information on the 11 changes to be trialled in the upcoming Ryan Cup Division 1 campaign. A twelfth change – a return to six substitutes – will not be experimented with as the higher education competition adopts an unlimited substitute policy. Major rule adjustments that will be trialled will include a four-point goal, a ban on fisted points unless the ball is in flight, a limit on consecutive handpasses to three, a backcourt rule while breach infractions will now be able to be taken outside the 40-metre arc for a two-point attempt. The EAG will assess the data and feedback after the Ryan Cup and former Mayo and Roscommon manager McStay is hopeful that a number of proposals are greenlit in time for next season's league campaign. "We'd like to see whatever stands up going straight into the league, and then they would be formalised at Congress. I think that's possible." McStay said that any change brought for ratification will only be approved on the back on rigorous examination from multiple stakeholders, a data perspective and, also, the eye-test.

stories.title: Klopp reluctant to weigh in on Manchester City fallout
stories.summary: Former Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp said his respect for Pep Guardiola and the Manchester City sides that battled Liverpool in some of the Premier League's closest title races has left him reluctant to comment on the fallout from City's financial rules case. City were found guilty of serious financial breaches by an independent commission on Tuesday, though the club have denied wrongdoing and are expected to appeal, with sanctions yet to be determined. The 59-year-old, whose Liverpool side twice finished a point behind City, had previously joked that he would attend a parade if Liverpool were retrospectively awarded titles but said he no longer felt that way. "I haven't given it much thought, even though I've seen it of course," Klopp told reporters on Wednesday. "I also know what I said about it in the past and how if there's ever a parade I'll be there, but it doesn't feel like that anymore. "My respect for Pep Guardiola and the football played at City during the time we played against each other... plus what an opponent they proved to be for us at the very highest level is far too great for me to be able to say anything now."

stories.title: Crowley targeting Christmas return amid injury layoff
stories.summary: Jack Crowley is still hoping to return to Munster action at some point over the festive period, but has acknowledged ongoing uncertainty on how his body will recover from a vascular lower limb injury that has kept him out since April. After missing the end of Munster's domestic campaign and Ireland’s Nations Championship tests in July, with the restart of the URC, Champions Cup and November internationals also coming too soon, the out-half says that a lengthy period on the sidelines has once again "highlighted my love for the game". As the start of this new season approached, Munster head coach Clayton McMillan confirmed that Crowley had suffered a "narrowing of a (blood) vessel". Crowley explained that the issue left him unable to run or kick a rugby ball, but that he was not hindered away from the pitch. "Please God that when it comes to Christmas, I’ll be fully fit," he said. "I’m currently in a period of just rest. It’s just allowing everything to heal, to get strong. From that period return to exercise. I can do upper body work but in terms of running and stuff, that’s not happening right now."

stories.title: Druid explores O'Neill's A Moon for the Misbegotten
stories.summary: Patrick Lonergan explores the history of Eugene O'Neill's theatrical masterpiece A Moon for the Misbegotten, revived by Druid Theatre Company and coming to Gaiety Theatre this October for the Dublin Theatre Festival. A Moon for the Misbegotten was the last play that Eugene O'Neill ever completed, and its elegiac tone makes it feel like it might have been his own unconscious farewell to playwriting. He described his play as a "fine, unusual, tragic comedy" – and its blend of humour and sadness is indeed both fine and unusual. The play is deeply autobiographical, drawing on the figure of O’Neill’s brother Jamie, an actor who had drunk himself to death when he was only 45. Reimagining his brother as James Tyrone, O’Neill confines that character to a single place and a single 24-hour-period, so that he can grapple with the possibility of finding love with Josie, a young Irish-American woman. What follows is a battle between both characters’ competing desires: for love, reputation, ownership of land – and for just one more drink. Irishness is central to those conflicts. The play’s stage directions say of Josie that the "map of Ireland is stamped on her face" – an old Irish-American saying that was intended to suggest distinctively Irish features. But in one of many connections between the two characters, the same phrasing is used to describe Tyrone too – not in Moon but in A Long Day’s Journey Into Night, a companion play that O’Neill wrote between 1939 and 1941, but which was not staged until after his death. That link reveals O’Neill’s desire to present Tyrone and Josie both as psychologically complex individuals and as emblematically Irish. Writing about them thus became a way for him to map Ireland, and to think about its multifaceted influence on American life. That theme is apparent from the first act, when Josie and her father – a tenant farmer called Phil Hogan – are trying to frighten off a neighbouring landowner. They do so by playing on the stereotypes associated with their nationality: they are buoyant and comical – but also menacing, as if their buffoonery could tip into violence at any moment. They are, in other words, like characters in a stage Irish play.

stories.title: Things to do in Dublin this weekend (October 2-4)
stories.summary: From Halloween headpieces to Baroque A Cappella, there is plenty happening in Dublin this weekend. BuzzFest - Phibsboro's Community, Sustainability & Biodiversity Festival - returns for its 10th year on Saturday, 3 October. The festival will run from 12.30pm to 4pm in the Scouts Hall (located behind the library) with an amazing selection of stalls, stands, talks, workshops, repair cafe, music, food and craic. This includes a Halloween headpiece workshop inspired by collage art and fuelled by love for scavenging. All materials provided. The workshop will last 40 minutes and is aimed at those 6+. Tickets €2 on Eventbrite. Eatyard brings a slice of Bavaria to Drumcondra this October, with a series of beers*, pretzels, music, bands, fun & games running from Sept 24th - Oct 24th at The Bernard Shaw. Expect a whole host of German games to dig your teeth into, including Stein-Holding competitions, Hasselhoff karaoke, Lederhösen Limbo, the spicy currywurst challenge, live music & much more. Tickets €16.97 on Eventbrite. The event is for those 20+. Dublin Mountains Festival (Féile na Sléibhte) runs from 1-10 October, celebrating nature through community-driven events. On Friday, 2 October, a walk and talk with tree planting at Barnaslingan Wood will take place, led by the Coillte team overseeing the Dublin Mountains Makeover project. Reserve a spot on Eventbrite. Mother x Absolut present Daytime Dance Party: The Doll Edition On Saturday, 3 October, The George will play host to a very special edition of the Daytime Dance Party series. Trans, intersex and non-binary people will be celebrated with a jam-packed lineup including Glamo, Shrem, Mars Montana, Ruth Kavanagh, Shaqira Knightly, Toni & Tony, Dr Count Evil, Anziety, and Queeen Marie. Tickets are €5.58, with ticket revenue going to the Transgender Equality Network Ireland.

stories.title: Pike receiving 'life-saving care' after botched execution
stories.summary: Christa Pike is critically ill and receiving "life-saving medical care" in a Nashville hospital hours after she survived two attempts to execute her with lethal injections, her lawyers said, renewing scrutiny of ⁠capital punishment in the US. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in the 1990s after being convicted of a murder she carried out as a teenager. Her botched execution on Wednesday at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, the second this year in Tennessee, highlights the difficulties US states face in carrying out lethal injections and finding suitable alternative methods of capital punishment. "Christa is alive right now," Randall Spivey, one of Pike's lawyers who was a witness at the execution attempt, told reporters on Thursday afternoon. "We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now." Her lawyers repeated their calls for Pike's sentence to be commuted to life in prison after enduring what they called "chemical torture."

stories.title: Drumcree parade dispute talks end without agreement
stories.summary: Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement, while the Garvaghy Road residents have temporarily postponed their court case challenging the parade. It was due to have been heard in Belfast's Court of Appeal tomorrow, but the court case has been pushed back to Monday. The residents had lodged a further appeal against the Parades Commission determination that said 35 Orangemen could walk along the Garvaghy Road on Sunday. It is believed the decision was taken to allow space for mediation, which took place this evening. British Secretary of State for Northern Ireland Chris Bryant said talks over the Drumcree dispute are between a "rock and a hard place". "We haven't come to a settled agreement and it's a shame but my door remains open obviously, tomorrow and in future days."

stories.title: Labour's budget plans focus on reducing household bills
stories.summary: Labour leader Ivana Bacik has said her party is "relentlessly focused on keeping household bills down in the cost of living crisis". Publishing its alternative budget, the party is proposing targeted energy credits worth €400 to households earning less than €80,000. Further measures to tackle the soaring cost of energy include the extension of excise reductions and the reduction of VAT on home heating oil to 9%. Labour says Ireland can afford to increase core social welfare payments by €15 per week - it also wants to increase public sector pay and index income tax rates and bands in line with a projected wage growth of 4%. Labour, along with other opposition parties, is suggesting a second, targeted rate of child benefit to, as it says, "lift tens of thousands of children out of poverty". Finance spokesperson, Ged Nash, said that "the very best way to make our country fit for the future means we must declare war on child poverty, and we must mean it".

stories.title: Global M&A deal rush fades in Q3 on higher borrowing cost
stories.summary: Global merger and acquisition activity in the third quarter totalled $993 billion, down 41% compared to the prior quarter, marking the first quarter to fall below $1 trillion since the second quarter of 2025, according to LSEG data. Banca Monte dei Paschi's $32 billion bid for Banco BPM and Gold Fields' $25.7 billion bid for Northern Star Resources were among the 10 deals over $10 billion announced in the third quarter, the lowest number of quarterly megadeals since the fourth quarter of 2024. While the boom in artificial intelligence and data centre building has lifted the outlook for economic growth, surging energy costs have been fanning inflation and pushing expectations higher about where interest rates will settle. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield hit 5.34% on Thursday, its highest level since 2002, after posting the biggest quarterly rise this century in the three months to September. "At the margins [higher yields] makes valuations sometimes a little tougher," said John Collins, global head of M&A at Morgan Stanley. "That said, the impact is hard to quantify, so I'm not ready to call a slowdown based on what we are seeing." So far this year worldwide M&A is up 28% to $3.9 trillion, the highest level in the period since 2001, while the number of deals fell 8%, levels not seen since 2020.

stories.title: Swiss glaciers suffer 'catastrophic' melt in 2026
stories.summary: Switzerland's glaciers, which are disproportionately impacted by climate change, have lost nearly 20% of their mass in five years, experts have said, with 2026 registering the second-biggest melt on record. Swiss glaciers saw 5.5% of their volume melt away this year, the Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland (GLAMOS) network found in a new study, published after a record hot summer preceded by a winter with little snowfall. "The glaciers this year have lost enormous quantities of ice," said GLAMOS chief Matthias Huss, describing 2026 as "a catastrophic year". Perched on the Scex Rouge glacier, at an altitude of nearly 3,000 metres, he gazed across the landscape in despair. He carefully dismantled the four-metre-long aluminium measurement stake inserted at the centre of the glacier. In late July, when it was installed, it was completely embedded, but now more than three metres protrude from the grey surface of the ice.

stories.title: Cooke stance contributed to Saturday's shambolic scenes
stories.summary: It's when issues become difficult, uncomfortable and potentially damaging that you find out most about the people running an organisation. Over the last number of months and particularly throughout this entire situation surrounding Ireland’s games against Israel I’ve become increasingly concerned by the leadership of FAI president Paul Cooke. This isn’t personal. I don’t know Paul well enough to make it personal. My concern is football. Irish football, and how it’s represented and led. More specifically, the decisions being made at the very top of the association, and whether they have the best interests of Irish football, its supporters and its players at their core. Last November the FAI General Assembly voted overwhelmingly to instruct the association to ask UEFA for the immediate suspension of the Israel Football Association over alleged breaches of UEFA and FIFA statutes.
